en: The Questions of King Milinda 1. The Discourse on the Commencement.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
That king named Milinda,
at Sāgalā, the most excellent city,
approached Nāgasena.
Just as the Ganges flows into the ocean,
so the king approached Citrakathi,
the bearer of light who dispels the darkness.
He asked many subtle questions concerning what is possible and what is impossible;
both the questions and their answers—
Dependent upon profound meaning,
reaching the heart, pleasant to the ear,
wonderful, and hair-raising.
Profound in its Abhidhamma and Vinaya,
complete with its web of Suttas,
the discourse of Nāgasena is variegated.
By means of similes and methods.
Having directed one's knowledge toward that,
and having gladdened the mind;
"Listen to these subtle questions,
which shatter the points of doubt.
This is as it is handed down in tradition:
There is among the Yonas a city named Sāgala, a diverse metropolis adorned by rivers and mountains,

a delightful region of the earth, endowed with parks, gardens, groves, ponds, and lotus-pools; it is charming with its rivers, mountains, and forests, built by those possessed of learning, with its enemies subdued and its adversaries oppressed,
possessing various and manifold strong watchtowers and ramparts, and featuring excellent and magnificent gate-towers and archways.
The inner city was surrounded by a white rampart with deep moats;
it featured well-laid-out streets, crossroads, squares, and junctions; its marketplaces were filled with various kinds of excellent goods displayed for sale;
it was graced by hundreds of foremost sites for various acts of giving; and it was adorned with hundreds of thousands of magnificent palaces resembling the peaks of the Himālaya mountains.

It was crowded with elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; frequented by throngs of handsome men and women; teeming with people and inhabitants; filled with many Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras;
packed with various assemblies of ascetics and Brāhmaṇas; long inhabited by men possessing manifold sciences; well-stocked with shops for various kinds of cloth such as Kāsika and Koṭumbarika;
possessing flower and perfume shops displaying many beautiful varieties of flowers and scents; fragrant with perfumes; and filled with many desirable jewels.
With its market stalls well-displayed facing every direction, frequented by throngs of elegant merchants,
filled with kahāpaṇas, silver, gold, bronze, and precious stones, it was a dwelling-place for shining treasures; abounding in wealth, grain, riches, and utensils,

with full treasuries and granaries, and plenty of food and drink— consisting of various kinds of snacks, hard foods, soft foods, drinks, and elixirs— it resembled Uttarakuru, with its abundant harvests.
It is like the city of the gods, Āḷakamandā.
Standing here, one should recount their past karma; and when recounting it, it should be told by dividing it into six parts.
Namely as follows:
The preliminary practice consists of the Milinda-pañha, the Lakkhaṇa-pañha, the Meṇḍaka-pañha, the Anumāna-pañha, and the Opamma-kathā-pañha.
Among these, the Milinda-pañha is twofold: the Lakkhaṇa-pañha and the Vimaticchedana-pañha.
The Meṇḍaka-pañha is also twofold: the Mahāvagga and the Yogikathā-pañha.
